questions.question: Why should you import `node:assert/strict` instead of plain `node:assert` in tests?
options: Only the strict variant supports async assertions
In legacy mode equal uses == so assert.equal(1, "1") passes; strict mode compares with Object.is
The plain module is not available inside node:test
Strict mode automatically generates coverage reports
questions.explanation: Legacy assert.equal and deepEqual use loose equality. The strict variant makes equal behave like strictEqual and deepEqual like deepStrictEqual.

questions.question: A test calls `assert.rejects(promise, /timeout/)` without `await`. What is the likely result?
options: The test may pass before the assertion has actually been checked
Node throws a SyntaxError at load time
The assertion runs synchronously, so nothing changes
The test runner automatically awaits it and reports correctly
questions.explanation: assert.rejects returns a promise. Without await (or returning it), the test function finishes first and a failed assertion can be missed.

questions.question: What is the advantage of using `t.mock.method(...)` from the test context instead of replacing the method by hand?
options: It makes the method run in a worker thread
It records calls and automatically restores the original method when the test ends
It is the only way to mock async functions
questions.explanation: Mocks created through the test context track calls in .mock.calls and are restored after the test, so they never leak into other tests.

questions.question: How do you test a 300 ms debounce with node:test without waiting in real time?
options: Pass a timeout option of 300 to it()
Enable mock.timers for setTimeout and call tick(300)
questions.explanation: mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] }) replaces timers with fake ones, and tick(ms) advances fake time instantly and deterministically.
